summary: Specifies how PCEP carries a Binding Segment Identifier (BSID), as described in RFC 8402. A BSID can be tied to an RSVP-TE signaled LSP or SR path so upstream nodes can steer traffic into it, helping scalability and service independence.

eli5.summary: A BSID is a nickname for a long route, so you can say just the nickname. This explains how the route planner passes that nickname around.

questions: how does pcep carry a binding sid
subtitle: How PCEP carries a binding label or SID, a short alias for a longer traffic-engineered path.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing uses Binding SIDs as shorthand for a path, but a PCE had no standard way to learn a binding label/SID from a PCC, or to ask a PCC to allocate one.
tldr.mechanism: A new optional TE-PATH-BINDING TLV (type 55) in the LSP object carries the binding value. A removal flag withdraws it, and a P flag lets the PCE allocate the value itself when PCECC is in use.
tldr.outcome: PCEs and PCCs can report, request and remove binding labels and SIDs for RSVP-TE and SR paths. RFC 9604 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 9604 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains the base specification for carrying binding labels and SIDs in PCEP, read together with that update.

sections.title: Binding SIDs and the Problem
sections.content:
Traffic engineering paths are set up with either RSVP-TE or Segment Routing (SR). In SR, a head-end steers traffic with an SR Policy, an ordered list of segments. A Binding SID (BSID) is bound to such a policy: packets whose active segment equals the BSID are steered onto the bound policy. The RFC uses the term binding label/SID for both SR and non-SR paths, and binding value for either an MPLS label or a SID.

A binding label/SID has local significance to the ingress node of the TE path. For a stateful PCE to build end-to-end policies, it needs to learn that value from the PCC, or to tell the PCC which value to use. This document defines the PCEP extension for that.
sections.eli5: A long list of directions can be given a short nickname. Other people can then just say the nickname instead of reading out every turn.

sections.title: Why a Binding SID Helps
sections.content:
The RFC's example is a data center connected to an IP/MPLS WAN. In the WAN, an SR-TE LSP uses the SID list {A, B, C, D}. The gateway Node-1, acting as PCC, allocates a binding SID X and reports it to the PCE. For the MPLS data center, the PCE gives the access node the stack {Y, X}, where Y is the node SID of Node-1.

Without the BSID, the PCE would have to hand the access node the whole stack {Y, A, B, C, D}. The BSID therefore reduces the number of SIDs imposed by access nodes with limited forwarding capacity.
sections.eli5: Instead of giving a delivery driver five separate turns to memorize, you give two: go to the depot, then take the route called X. The depot already knows what X means.

sections.title: The TE-PATH-BINDING TLV
sections.content:
The optional TE-PATH-BINDING TLV has type 55 and variable length. It is carried in the LSP object (and may appear in the PCEP-ERROR object on errors), and several may be present. It holds a Binding Type (BT), a Flags byte, a Reserved field that MUST be zero, and the binding value, padded with zeros to a 4-octet boundary.

  • BT = 0: a 20-bit MPLS label (Length MUST be 7).
  • BT = 1: a 32-bit MPLS Label Stack Entry with label, Traffic Class, S and TTL (Length MUST be 8).
  • BT = 2: a 16-octet SRv6 SID (Length MUST be 20).
  • BT = 3: a 24-octet field with the SRv6 SID plus its Endpoint Behavior and SID Structure (Length MUST be 28).

The one defined flag is R (Removal): set means the peer requires the binding to be removed, unset means it is added or retained. For SRv6, the RFC RECOMMENDS always using BT = 3. The structure lengths (locator block, locator node, function, arguments) must total at most 128 bits, otherwise the TLV is invalid and a PCErr with Error-Type 10 and Error-value 37 MUST be sent.
sections.eli5: It is a small labeled box. One part says what kind of nickname is inside, one part is a remove-this switch, and the rest holds the nickname itself.

sections.title: Reporting, Requesting and Removing Bindings
sections.content:
Usually the PCC allocates the binding value and reports it to the PCE in a PCRpt message. To withdraw it, the PCC sends a PCRpt with the TLV's R flag set. To change it, the PCC withdraws the old value and includes a new TLV with the new one.

A PCE can ask the PCC to use a specific value by sending a PCUpd or PCInitiate with a TE-PATH-BINDING TLV. If the PCC finds the value invalid it MUST send Error-Type 32 ("Binding label/SID failure") with Error-value 1; if it cannot allocate it, Error-value 2. A PCE can instead send an empty TLV (Length 4) to let the PCC pick its own value, and Error-value 3 is used if the PCC cannot allocate one. Error-value 4 covers a failed removal, and Error-value 5 covers the same value sent with inconsistent binding types.

If any TLV in a message causes an error, the whole message is rejected. A PCC that receives the TLV in a message other than PCUpd or PCInitiate (or a PCE in one other than PCRpt) MUST close the session as a malformed message.
sections.eli5: The router can tell the planner its nickname, ask to erase it, or swap it for a new one. The planner can also ask for a certain nickname, and the router says no if it cannot use it.

sections.title: Binding SIDs in Explicit Routes
sections.content:
Route information in PCEP is carried in the Explicit Route Object (ERO). RFC 8664 defines the SR-ERO subobject, which can include a Node or Adjacency Identifier (NAI) identified by an NAI Type (NT). When the SID is a binding SID, the NAI MUST NOT be included and NT MUST be set to zero.

The same rule applies to the SRv6-ERO subobject defined in RFC 9603. Section 5.2.1 of RFC 8664 gives the bit settings and error handling for NT = 0.
sections.eli5: When a step in the route is a nickname, you do not add the street address next to it. The nickname stands alone.

sections.title: Letting the PCE Allocate the Value
sections.content:
When the PCE acts as a central controller (PCECC, RFC 9050) and manages part of the label space, it may allocate the binding label/SID itself. Both peers need to have exchanged the PCECC capability first. A new P (PCE-allocation) flag in the LSP object signals this.

  • PCE allocates: it sets P=1 and includes the TLV with a value in a PCInitiate or PCUpd.
  • PCC allocates: the PCE sets P=0, with an empty TLV if it wants the PCC to choose.
  • PCC asks the PCE to allocate: it sets P=1 and D=1 with an empty TLV in a PCRpt, and the PCE answers with a PCUpd carrying the value.

If either side has not advertised PCECC support and receives P=1, it MUST send Error-Type 19 with Error-value 16 and terminate the session. A legacy speaker that does not know the P flag ignores it.
sections.eli5: Usually the router picks its own nickname. If both sides agree the planner is in charge of nicknames, the planner can pick it, and a flag says who did.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 8231, RFC 8281, RFC 8664 and RFC 9050 apply. The RFC points out that binding SIDs are shorthand aliases whose expansion is known only to the node acting on it. Here the expansion is shared between PCC and PCE, so a rogue PCC or PCE could shift or misdirect traffic in ways that are hard for other nodes to detect, for instance by substituting a BSID from a different LSP.

With BT = 3, the SID Structure cannot be validated, and shifting bits into or out of the argument field can change how bits are processed. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS activating these extensions only on authenticated and encrypted sessions between PCEs and PCCs of the same administrative authority, using TLS as in RFC 8253.
sections.eli5: A nickname hides what is behind it. If someone dishonest swaps a nickname, traffic could go to the wrong place without anyone noticing, so only trusted, protected conversations should use this.
